content: The diseases caused by different viruses are not related to one another. Humans cannot contract diseases from animals, and animals cannot contract diseases from humans. Hand, Foot, and Mouth Disease (HFMD) Geographical Distribution: HFMD occurs worldwide and is increasingly prevalent in the Asia-Pacific region. Causative Agents: HFMD is caused by viruses belonging to the Enterovirus genus of the Picornaviridae family. Specific serotypes include Coxsackievirus and Enterovirus 71 (EV71). Clinical Concerns: EV71 infections are particularly concerning as they can lead to severe disease in children, sometimes resulting in death. Risk Factors: Poor hygiene and direct contact with infected individuals are significant risk factors. Children under 10 years, especially those under 5, are at the highest risk. Transmission: HFMD is highly contagious and spreads through direct contact with nasal and throat secretions, saliva, blister fluid, or stool of infected individuals. Patients are most infectious during the febrile phase. Symptoms: After an incubation period of 3–7 days, symptoms include fluid-filled blisters on the hands, feet, and inside the mouth, as well as dehydration due to fever and poor fluid intake. Severe outbreaks caused by EV71 can lead to neurological complications such as meningoencephalitis, pneumonia, and myocarditis, which may result in significant mortality. In contrast, outbreaks caused by Coxsackievirus A16 are not associated with severe complications or mortality. Treatment: Management is symptomatic and supportive. Prevention: Hand hygiene is critical. Wash hands with soap or use alcohol-based sanitizers before eating, feeding a baby, or preparing food. Disinfect contaminated surfaces and items, including toys. Avoid close contact with infected individuals. Japanese Encephalitis (JE) Geographical Distribution: JE is primarily found in the Asia-Pacific region, with approximately 60% of the global population living in endemic areas. Causative Agent: JE is caused by a virus from the Flavivirus genus in the Flaviviridae family. Vectors and Reservoirs: The virus is transmitted by mosquitoes, particularly Culex tritaeniorhynchus and Culex vishnui. It circulates in ardeid birds (herons and egrets) and amplifies in pigs, which do not develop disease but infect mosquitoes that bite them. Human Infection: Humans are accidental hosts, infected when bitten by infected mosquitoes. Children in endemic areas are at higher risk, especially during and after the monsoon season when mosquito populations peak. Symptoms: After an incubation period of 5–15 days, symptoms include sudden high fever, stiff neck, coma, tremors, and convulsions, particularly in infants. Severe cases can lead to permanent central nervous system damage or death, with a case-fatality rate of 25–30%. Treatment: There is no specific treatment, but supportive care and good nursing can reduce mortality. Prevention: Prevent mosquito bites by wearing protective clothing and using insect repellents. Mass immunization of children and pigs in endemic areas is recommended, as is vaccination for travelers to these regions. Nipah Virus (NiV) Geographical Distribution: NiV outbreaks have been reported in Bangladesh, India, Malaysia, and Singapore. Causative Agent: Nipah virus belongs to the Paramyxoviridae family. Reservoirs: Fruit bats of the genus Pteropus (flying foxes) are the primary reservoirs. The virus can infect pigs, dogs, cats, horses, and humans through contact with bat secretions (saliva, urine) or contaminated food. Human Infection: In Bangladesh, drinking raw date palm sap contaminated by bats is a major risk factor. Human-to-human transmission has been reported, particularly among healthcare workers exposed to infected patients' secretions, excretions, blood, or tissues. Symptoms: The incubation period is 4–21 days. Symptoms range from asymptomatic infection to fatal encephalitis. Initial symptoms include fever, headache, muscle pain, vomiting, and sore throat, followed by dizziness, drowsiness, altered consciousness, and acute encephalitis. Severe cases may involve atypical pneumonia, acute respiratory distress, seizures, and coma, with a case-fatality rate of 40–75%. Treatment: There is no vaccine or specific treatment. Intensive supportive care is the main approach. Prevention: Avoid contact with bats and bat-contaminated food. Healthcare workers should use standard precautions, including gloves and masks, when caring for suspected or confirmed cases. Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome (SARS) Geographical Distribution: SARS first appeared in Guangdong, China, in 2002 and spread to 26 countries, causing over 8,000 cases in 2003. Causative Agent: SARS is caused by the SARS coronavirus (SARS-CoV). Reservoirs: Initially thought to be civet cats, bats are now considered the primary reservoir, with civet cats acting as intermediate hosts. Symptoms: After an incubation period of 2–14 days, symptoms include sudden flu-like illness with fever, muscle pain, lethargy, cough, and sore throat. Severe cases progress to respiratory disease and pneumonia, which can be fatal. Treatment: No specific treatment exists. Symptomatic and supportive therapy is required. Prevention: Isolate suspected cases, wear protective clothing when handling patients, and follow disease control guidelines. Middle East Respiratory Syndrome (MERS) Geographical Distribution: MERS cases have been reported in 11 countries, primarily in the Middle East, with all cases linked to the region. Causative Agent: MERS is caused by the MERS coronavirus (MERS-CoV). Reservoirs: The virus is believed to be of animal origin, with camels identified as a likely source of human infection. Symptoms: The incubation period is 2–10 days. Most patients present with respiratory illness, including fever, cough, and breathing difficulties. Pneumonia is common, and severe complications include kidney failure and acute respiratory distress. Treatment: No specific treatment is available. Supportive care is the mainstay of management. Prevention: Basic hygiene measures, such as frequent handwashing, avoiding sick animals, and ensuring food safety, are recommended. Healthcare workers should follow infection prevention protocols when treating MERS patients.
